summary: The Network Information Center announces that it is compiling a list of reports from ARPANET sites that matter to participants. This includes reports from ARPA information processing contracts, project hardware and software, and general site reports. Sites were asked to help identify and supply them.

plainLanguage.summary: A library says it wants to collect every report written by the groups on the network. They ask sites to tell them what exists and send copies.

subtitle: Building a network-wide bibliography of site research reports.

tldr.problem: As the ARPANET grew, research was being conducted at many sites but there was no central catalog of what reports and papers existed, making it hard for network participants to learn about each other's work.
tldr.mechanism: The Network Information Center began compiling a comprehensive list of site-produced reports, bibliographies, and research papers. Sites were asked to identify, describe, and contribute copies of reports produced under ARPA contracts and of general interest to the network.
tldr.outcome: The NIC created a centralized collection and bibliography of network research, allowing sites to refer report requests to NIC for handling and providing researchers with a comprehensive reference tool.

today: RFC 182 is a foundational step toward what became the RFC index and later comprehensive internet archives. The NIC's approach of centralized curation with distributed contribution established a pattern still used by institutions like the Internet Archive and digital libraries worldwide.

sections.title: The Need for a Network Bibliography
sections.content:
RFC 182 announces that the Network Information Center is working to compile a list of all site-produced reports of interest to ARPANET participants. The effort includes reports produced under ARPA Information Processing Technology contracts, as well as reports on network planning, project hardware and software, and the general subject areas of individual sites.

In an initial effort, the NIC had requested site agents to send copies of existing bibliographies of their site's reports. However, other responsibilities had occupied the NIC's time. In the meantime, some sites had sent lists of their reports, and work by Peggy Karp had covered much of the ground. Demand for a comprehensive compilation of references and an accessible collection of the actual reports had grown.
sections.plainLanguage: The network was producing lots of research papers. The information center wanted to gather them all in one place so people could find what others were working on.

sections.title: NIC Responsibilities and Services
sections.content:
The NIC assumed responsibility for satisfying the network's demand for research reports. The center would provide sites with access to other sites' reports, allowing sites to refer requests for their own reports to the NIC for centralized handling. Requests from inside or outside the ARPANET for reports produced under ARPA IPT contracts could be forwarded or referred to the NIC.

For requests from outside the network, the NIC would not attempt to supply copies directly but would answer the request with information for ordering from the government (where known) or refer the request to the report's originator.

The NIC would also provide all sites and external researchers with bibliographic tools to facilitate reference to network reports. This centralized approach avoided duplicating effort and created a single authoritative source for discovering ARPANET research.
sections.plainLanguage: The information center would keep copies, help people find reports, answer questions about what was available, and direct requests to the right site if needed.

sections.title: Call for Site Participation
sections.content:
RFC 182 makes explicit requests of the ARPANET sites. The NIC would appreciate receiving any existing bibliographies of relevant site-produced reports. Additionally, sites are requested to place the NIC on their distribution lists for new relevant reports, ensuring that the bibliography stays current as research progresses.

This participatory model turned information collection into a shared responsibility: the NIC served as the central aggregator and curator, but sites contributed by documenting their work and ensuring new reports reached the center.
sections.plainLanguage: Each site was asked to send copies of what they published and to tell the information center about new work so the bibliography would stay up to date.
